title: Improving Reasoning with Rollout Agreement for Group-Based Policy Optimization
authors: Sohyun Son, Yerim Hong, Jaeyun Park, Mujeen Sung
abstract: Recent methods for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) use rollout diversity to improve reasoning performance or training efficiency. Despite these gains, the extent to which differences among correct-answer rollouts reflect useful alternative reasoning or unresolved errors remains poorly understood. We investigate this question through a blind paired analysis of a model trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), comparing the highest- and lowest-agreement correct-answer traces for the same problem. Across 126 pairs, low-agreement traces have more spurious reasoning than high-agreement traces (35% vs. 22%), including internal inconsistencies and misuse of problem conditions. Based on these findings, we propose RoAR (Rollout-Agreement Reward), which adds reasoning-level agreement to GRPO's rewards for verified-correct rollouts. RoAR computes this signal from existing on-policy rollout groups, requiring no human-written rationales, additional sampling, or separately trained process evaluator. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the 1.5B GRPO-RoAR model reaches 55.5% mean pass@1 under zero-shot evaluation using 7K training examples, exceeding GRPO and GRPO-CARE by 6.0 and 5.5 percentage points. A separate blind audit of 100 problems answered correctly by all four 1.5B models finds spurious rates of 18% for GRPO-RoAR, 32% for GRPO, 27% for GRPO-CARE, and 37% for DRA-GRPO. Our findings identify reasoning validity as an important consideration when using rollout differences to guide learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/ldi-kyunghee/RoAR.

infographic.key_insight: Correct answers can mask flawed reasoning; rewarding agreement among reasoning traces improves both mathematical accuracy and reasoning validity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RoAR adds a reasoning-agreement reward to GRPO using existing on-policy rollouts, without extra sampling, human-written rationales, or a separately trained process evaluator.
method: Blindly compare high- and low-agreement correct-answer traces for the same problem.
Add reasoning-level agreement rewards to verified-correct rollouts.
Train with GRPO-RoAR and evaluate accuracy and spurious reasoning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five math benchmarks, the 1.5B GRPO-RoAR model achieved 55.5% mean zero-shot pass@1 after training on 7K examples, beating GRPO by 6.0 percentage points; a separate 100-problem audit found 18% spurious reasoning versus GRPO's 32%.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement is not proof of valid reasoning: the reported audit still found spurious reasoning in 18% of GRPO-RoAR traces and covered only problems answered correctly by all four models.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Reasoning with Rollout Agreement for Group-Based Policy Optimization

title: Unit: a type checker for dependent type theory
abstract: We present Unit, a type checker for dependent type theory with a module system in the tradition of Automath and a uniform treatment of definitions: two uses of a definition are compared by name and arguments before anything is unfolded, and otherwise the definition declared last is opened. There is no unification, no instance search, no tactics and no unfolding heuristic, so the work of checking can be observed and compared with the informal proof. With Unit we have checked a model of univalent type theory, synthetic algebraic geometry up to Châtelet's theorem, and synthetic Stone duality with its cohomology. These developments show that a small, uniform system supports substantial mathematics, and give concrete reasons to reconsider the complexity routinely accepted in proof assistants.

infographic.key_insight: Unit shows that a small dependent-type checker with uniform definition handling can support substantial formal mathematics without tactics, unification, or instance search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its explicit checking process offers a simpler architecture for proof-checking tools whose behavior can be inspected alongside informal proofs.
method: Use dependent type theory with an Automath-style module system.
Compare definitions by name and arguments before unfolding; otherwise unfold the most recently declared definition.
Avoid unification, instance search, tactics, and unfolding heuristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports checked developments covering a model of univalent type theory, synthetic algebraic geometry through Châtelet’s theorem, and synthetic Stone duality with its cohomology, but gives no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The lack of proof automation may increase manual proof-authoring effort; the abstract does not quantify this trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Unit: a type checker for dependent type theory

title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization
abstract: By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(Δx^2 + Δy^2 + Δt^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.

infographic.key_insight: ADACT jointly optimizes processor workload throttling and cooling to manage temperature while balancing execution throughput and cooling energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-informed thermal control could help AI and HPC processors sustain performance under power-density and temperature constraints.
method: Model chip temperature with a 2D reaction–diffusion PDE, localized power sources, and variable convective cooling.
Discretize using Crank–Nicolson time stepping and a five-point spatial stencil.
Compute control gradients with a backward adjoint and optimize using L-BFGS.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports second-order forward and adjoint convergence verified by manufactured solutions, gradient checks via Taylor tests, and numerical experiments maintaining thermal thresholds and throughput.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is numerical; real-time deployment and robustness to chip-model mismatch are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization

title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning
abstract: A central limitation of modern machine learning systems is the lack of formal certificates guaranteeing their behavior beyond empirical, sample-based evaluation. Sum-of-squares (SOS) methods provide such guarantees by certifying polynomial inequalities over continuous domains via semidefinite programming (SDP). While prior work has introduced SDP layers as differentiable components in neural networks, repeated learning calls can lose the computational benefit of the forward program's sparse representation. We propose Sparse SOS Layers, differentiable value layers whose backward passes reuse the local coordinates of the forward solve. Under a fixed template and learned objective coefficients, each layer avoids building dense certificates and reuses its sparse structure across training steps. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves up to 2.7 times speedup in total warm-call time, with nearly 100 times lower memory usage (1.7 vs. 160 GiB) for relatively large problem sizes for the tested dense parameterization. Experiments cover sparse polynomial certification, pendulum control, combinatorial relaxations, robotics projection, oscillator chains, and pose graph synchronization. A design study achieves zero certified violations across unseen problem instances and sizes, while requiring roughly 7 times fewer optimization solves than estimating gradients by perturbing the objective coefficients and re-solving the problem (finite differences). These results show that sparse certificate values can be effectively integrated into learning pipelines when the backward pass respects the verifier's structure.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse SOS Layers make polynomial certification differentiable while preserving the forward solver’s sparse structure during backpropagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: They enable learning pipelines to incorporate formal certificates over continuous domains with lower runtime and memory costs than the tested dense approach.
method: Certify polynomial inequalities using sum-of-squares semidefinite programs.
Learn objective coefficients within a fixed certificate template.
Reuse local sparse coordinates in backward passes without constructing dense certificates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six application areas, experiments report up to 2.7× faster total warm calls and 1.7 versus 160 GiB memory usage; a design study reports zero certified violations on unseen instances and sizes with roughly 7× fewer solves than finite differences.
infographic.watch_item: The approach assumes a fixed template with learned objective coefficients; performance gains may depend on problem sparsity and the chosen parameterization.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning

title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models
authors: Edric Tam, Qingyang Liu, Barbara Engelhardt, Ray Bai
abstract: Broad classes of deep generative models (DGMs) operate by learning to map a simple source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, to a complex high-dimensional target distribution. Despite their success, DGMs often empirically struggle to accurately represent distributions with heavy tails or well-separated modes. In this work, we show that these difficulties reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying transport problem rather than particular neural network architectures or training procedures. We establish quantitative lower bounds on the gradients and Jacobians of pushforward mappings that transport log-concave source distributions to such targets. For heavy-tailed target distributions, the required gradient magnitude grows as the target develops increasingly large moments. For multimodal target distributions, the low-probability regions between well-separated modes similarly force large gradients in the transport map. We discuss how such large derivatives relate to trade-offs between expressivity and numerical stability. Our results hold under substantially weaker regularity conditions than previous analyses and remain stable under perturbations of the target distribution. Finally, we show that these obstructions can be mitigated when the goal is approximation of a given density rather than generative modeling. Specifically, we propose simple classes of bijective reparametrizations that can alleviate the difficult geometric structure and reduce the gradient burden placed on the learned generative map. Numerical experiments support our theoretical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Transporting a simple log-concave source to heavy-tailed or well-separated multimodal targets intrinsically requires large gradients, regardless of the generative model’s architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These gradient barriers create expressivity–stability trade-offs that architecture or training changes alone may not resolve.
method: Derive quantitative gradient and Jacobian lower bounds for pushforward maps.
Establish barriers under weaker regularity assumptions and target perturbations.
Propose bijective reparametrizations to reduce gradient demands in density approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis, but the abstract provides no datasets, metrics, or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The reparametrization mitigation concerns density approximation and should not be assumed to remove barriers in generative sampling.
infographic.paper_title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models

title: Constraint Learning by Optimizing over Trained Neural Networks: A Pragmatic Tutorial
abstract: Constraint learning is an emerging paradigm of modeling optimization problems with the help of machine learning. In this paradigm, trained machine learning models are embedded into the optimization model. For example, we can learn constraints empirically from available data, or we can avoid using a nonlinear objective function by learning a simpler approximation for it. Neural networks become a compelling option if the machine learning models must capture more elaborate and nuanced relationships. However, optimization models embedding neural networks may become too large or too slow to solve. In this tutorial, we present practical considerations for an effective and efficient use of constraint learning with neural networks and validate it with a case study highlighting the benefit of smaller and sparser networks.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding trained neural networks into optimization models can capture complex relationships, but smaller, sparser networks can make the resulting problems easier to solve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can use learned constraints or objective approximations to model data-driven systems while balancing predictive fidelity against optimization cost.
method: Train neural networks to represent empirical constraints or approximate nonlinear objectives.
Embed the trained networks into an optimization model.
Consider smaller, sparser networks to improve computational tractability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a case study highlighting the benefit of smaller and sparser networks, without specifying datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Embedding neural networks can produce optimization models that are too large or too slow to solve.
infographic.paper_title: Constraint Learning by Optimizing over Trained Neural Networks: A Pragmatic Tutorial

title: Understanding Practical Optimization in Machine Learning
abstract: Modern machine learning relies on practical optimization methods that often differ from the algorithms studied in classical analyses: they train submodels, clip or normalize gradients, use layer-wise non-Euclidean directions, or approximate costly inner computations. This thesis analyzes the objective, assumptions, update, and computation defined by these procedures, rather than those of simplified proxies. For submodel training, we show that Independent Subnetwork Training can converge to a shifted fixed point because sketching before differentiation biases the update for the original objective. Model-Agnostic Sparsified Training instead incorporates the sketch distribution into its objective, which makes sketched gradients unbiased and admits convergence guarantees. For private optimization, we show that adaptive quantile clipping retains bias at any fixed quantile, while suitable quantile schedules recover near-optimal nonconvex rates under heavy-tailed noise. We then combine smoothed normalization with error compensation and obtain distributed private convergence guarantees under standard assumptions, without assuming bounded gradients. For optimizers based on linear minimization oracles, we develop and validate a layer-wise generalized smoothness model and build on it the Gluon framework for Muon- and Scion-style methods. We also show that the approximate orthogonalization in Muon matters: less precise orthogonalization calls for smaller stepsizes, so its precision should be tuned together with the learning rate. Overall, practical methods are better understood when theory retains the features that determine their optimization behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Optimization theory better explains practical machine learning when it preserves the actual objectives, gradient transformations, layer-wise geometry, and computational approximations used in training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable training requires aligning sketching with the objective, scheduling clipping appropriately, and tuning approximate orthogonalization precision jointly with the learning rate.
method: Analyze submodel training to distinguish biased updates from unbiased gradients of sketch-aware objectives.
Study quantile clipping and combine smoothed normalization with error compensation for private optimization.
Develop layer-wise generalized smoothness and the Gluon framework for Muon- and Scion-style methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence guarantees, fixed-point bias analysis, and validation of a layer-wise smoothness model, but names no datasets or numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Coarser Muon orthogonalization requires smaller stepsizes, so reducing computation without retuning the learning rate may compromise optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Understanding Practical Optimization in Machine Learning

title: Lie Symmetry-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), with broad applications in physics, engineering, and medicine. However, their performance is highly sensitive to the sampling strategy for training points. Conventional uniform sampling often fails to adequately resolve regions with complex solution features, leading to low efficiency and limited accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a Lie symmetry-driven adaptive sampling framework for PINNs, termed Lie-AS-ISC. For PDEs admitting Lie symmetry groups, symmetry transformations are exploited to derive intrinsic functional relationships between the solution and its variables, enabling the construction of basis points with exact solutions that span the solution domain. Building on this, an adaptive sampling strategy is developed by jointly considering absolute error and invariant surface conditions, while a dual-index loss is introduced to enhance training constraints. The proposed method significantly improves prediction accuracy. The experimental results show that this method consistently outperforms existing methods in accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Lie-AS-ISC uses PDE Lie symmetries to guide adaptive sampling and improve physics-informed neural network accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-guided sampling could improve PINN-based PDE solvers for physics and engineering problems where uniform sampling misses complex solution features.
method: Use Lie symmetry transformations to derive solution–variable relationships and construct basis points with exact solutions.
Adapt training-point sampling using both absolute error and invariant surface conditions.
Introduce a dual-index loss to strengthen training constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistently higher accuracy than existing methods, but provides no benchmark details or numerical improvements.
infographic.watch_item: Application depends on usable PDE Lie symmetries and the ability to construct the required exact-solution basis points.
infographic.paper_title: Lie Symmetry-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference
abstract: Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization often predict solutions directly or use predictions to restrict search, while expressive energy-based models typically rely on approximate inference. We introduce EnerGNN, a framework that learns energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer programming (MIP). EnerGNN combines a graph neural network encoder with an optimization-compatible readout and a nonlinear energy head, enabling exact constrained inference over the learned energy. An optimality-aware contrastive loss trains the energy to reflect solution quality and constraint violations. Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem, EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility. On the supply chain problem, it achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and a 17.4$\times$ speedup over the monolithic MIP. The learned energy also generalizes to larger instances and supports zero-shot constraint injection, adapting to changing constraints without retraining while preserving feasibility.

infographic.key_insight: EnerGNN learns energy functions over binary configurations that can be minimized exactly under explicit hard constraints using mixed integer programming.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports feasible combinatorial decisions and zero-shot constraint changes without retraining, making it relevant to adaptive engineering planning.
method: Encode problem instances with a graph neural network.
Combine an optimization-compatible readout with a nonlinear energy head.
Train with an optimality-aware contrastive loss, then minimize learned energy under hard constraints using MIP.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and personalized cell therapy supply chain evaluations, EnerGNN reports near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility; the supply chain task achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and 17.4× speedup over monolithic MIP.
infographic.watch_item: Exact minimization of the learned energy does not guarantee optimality for the original objective, and MIP runtime may remain a scaling bottleneck.
infographic.paper_title: EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference

title: Affine-invariant Cubic Newton with Weak Learners
authors: Nikita Zozoulenko, Daniel Falkowski, Thomas Cass, Lukas Gonon
abstract: Modern gradient boosting algorithms are based on Newton's method, which excels empirically but lacks global convergence guarantees. While recent work on Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) boosting achieved a global $\mathcal{O}(1/γ^{12}k^2)$ rate, its analysis was not able to exploit the natural Hessian geometry and suffers from a heavy $γ^{12}$ dependence on a worst-case `weak gradient edge' $γ$. In this paper, we tackle these theoretical drawbacks by generalizing the Affine-Invariant Cubic Newton (AICN) scheme to convex optimization with weak learners. Our analysis is based on average cosine values $\overlineΘ_k$ along the optimization path and directional improvements $δ_k$ in the Hessian-induced norm. We show that the weak-AICN update reduces to a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by $δ_k$. Under semi-strong self-concordance, we establish a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\overlineΘ_k^4 k^2)$ rate, significantly improving upon the weak-GRN bound. We further prove a local linear rate, global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, cosine angle lower bounds, and present weak-AdaAICN, which adaptively tunes the cubic regularization. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of this framework beyond gradient boosting by showing that Newton coordinate descent emerges naturally as a special case of optimization with weak learners.

infographic.key_insight: Weak-AICN extends affine-invariant cubic Newton optimization to weak learners, achieving a global O(1/(Θ̄_k⁴k²)) convergence rate based on average pathwise cosine alignment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides convergence guarantees for Newton-style boosting and includes Newton coordinate descent as a special case.
method: Use Hessian geometry to measure weak-learner alignment and directional improvement.
Compute a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by directional improvement δ_k.
Adapt cubic regularization with weak-AdaAICN.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical global and local convergence guarantees, including global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The global rate assumes convexity and semi-strong self-concordance, and its practical value depends on weak learners maintaining useful pathwise alignment.
infographic.paper_title: Affine-invariant Cubic Newton with Weak Learners

title: Autonomous Structural Discovery Of Bioprocess Dynamics And Kinetics Via LLM-Driven Agents
abstract: High-fidelity digital twins in continuous biomanufacturing are often bottlenecked by incomplete kinetic models, while standard data-driven algorithms (e.g., SINDy, PINNs) lack interpretability or impose rigid physical assumptions. This paper introduces a hybrid closed-loop architecture for autonomous kinetic state-space discovery driven by a Large Language Model (LLM) agent. The framework employs a sequential "isolation-peeling" methodology across orthogonal operational regimes. This algorithmic peeling mathematically decouples entangled multiplicative (inhibitory) and additive (catalytic) biological rate law. Grounded in a Two-Level Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) library, the framework utilizes Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) and logarithmic decomposition to decouple complex cell growth kinetics into orthogonal multiplicative (inhibitory) and additive (regulatory) residual channels. When statistical degeneracy occurs an Active Design of Experiments (DoE) controller dynamically triggers targeted perturbations to decorrelate competing model hypotheses. Evaluated on a continuous stirred-tank reactor exhibiting unmodeled Haldane inhibition, Luong product toxicity, and secondary metabolite autocatalysis, the framework autonomously expanded the state space and recovered ground-truth parameters with under 6% error without a priori kinetic knowledge.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-driven closed loop discovers interpretable bioprocess dynamics by sequentially isolating entangled kinetic effects and expanding the modeled state space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve digital twins for continuous biomanufacturing when missing kinetic mechanisms limit model fidelity.
method: Ground an LLM agent in a two-level retrieval-augmented knowledge library.
Combine moving horizon estimation, logarithmic decomposition, and isolation-peeling across operating regimes to separate kinetic effects.
Trigger targeted experimental perturbations when competing model hypotheses remain statistically indistinguishable.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a continuous stirred-tank reactor evaluation with unmodeled Haldane inhibition, Luong product toxicity, and secondary metabolite autocatalysis, the framework recovered ground-truth parameters with under 6% error.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish robustness on real biomanufacturing data, where noise and safety constraints may limit informative perturbations.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous Structural Discovery Of Bioprocess Dynamics And Kinetics Via LLM-Driven Agents

title: Convergence Analysis of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent under Relaxed Assumptions
abstract: We study convergence rates of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent (NAG) method for convex optimization in both deterministic and stochastic settings. We focus on a more general smoothness condition raised from several machine learning problems empirically and theoretically. We show the accelerated convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\left(1/T^2\right)$ in terms of the function value gap, given access to exact gradients of objective functions, matching the optimal rate for standard smooth convex optimization in \citep{nesterov1983method}. Under the relaxed affine-variance noise assumption for stochastic optimization, we establish the high-probability convergence rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log\left(1/δ\right)/T}\right)$ and this rate could improve to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\log\left(1/δ\right)/T^2\right)$ when the noise parameters are sufficiently small. Here, $T$ denotes the total number of iterations and $δ$ is the probability margin. Up to logarithm factors, our probabilistic convergence rate reaches the same order of the expected rate obtained in \citep{ghadimi2016accelerated} where the assumptions of bounded variance noise and Lipschitz smoothness are required. We additionally establish the convergence rates of the studied algorithms in the non-convex setting.

infographic.key_insight: Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient Descent retains an O(1/T²) convex function-gap rate under relaxed smoothness, with high-probability stochastic guarantees under affine-variance noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis supports accelerated optimization in machine-learning settings where standard Lipschitz smoothness and bounded-variance noise assumptions may be too restrictive.
method: Analyze deterministic NAG under a generalized smoothness condition.
Establish stochastic convergence bounds under affine-variance noise.
Extend convergence analysis to non-convex objectives.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical rates: O(1/T²) with exact gradients and Õ(√(log(1/δ)/T)) with stochastic gradients, improving to Õ(log(1/δ)/T²) for sufficiently small noise parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The faster stochastic rate requires sufficiently small noise parameters; the abstract provides no empirical validation or implementation guidance.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent under Relaxed Assumptions

title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
abstract: The Stochastic Transport in Upper Ocean Dynamics project introduced a new paradigm for representing uncertainty in geophysical fluid dynamics through stochastic transport models calibrated from data. This paper provides a synthesis of the principal theoretical and data assimilation developments achieved as part of the project. The central theme of the paper is the transformation of stochastic transport models from a modelling paradigm into a mathematically rigorous framework equipped with analytical, variational, calibration and Bayesian data assimilation methodologies suitable for geophysical fluid dynamics. We describe the development of the theory of stochastic transport equations, including well-posedness, regularity and approximation results, together with their geometric foundations based on stochastic variational principles, rough paths and fractional transport models. We further review methodologies for calibrating stochastic transport structures from observational and high-resolution simulation data, ranging from reduced-order stochastic models to modern generative approaches. Finally, we discuss Bayesian inference and high-dimensional data assimilation techniques developed for stochastic transport models, including particle filter methodologies and machine learning uncertainty quantification. Taken together, these developments establish a coherent framework linking stochastic transport modelling, rigorous analysis, calibration and Bayesian inference, thereby providing a foundation for uncertainty quantification and forecasting in geophysical fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: This synthesis links stochastic transport models with rigorous analysis, data-driven calibration and high-dimensional Bayesian inference for uncertainty-aware geophysical forecasting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty quantification and data assimilation in geophysical fluid simulations, with potential value for ocean forecasting.
method: Establish well-posedness, regularity and approximation theory for stochastic transport equations.
Calibrate transport uncertainty using observations, high-resolution simulations, reduced-order models and generative approaches.
Apply particle filtering and machine-learning uncertainty quantification to Bayesian data assimilation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reviews theory and calibration using observational and simulation data, but reports no quantitative benchmarks or forecasting gains.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and calibration reliability in high-dimensional operational models require validation beyond the abstract's synthesis.
infographic.paper_title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.

infographic.key_insight: dSpark accelerates diffusion language models by learning when to reveal tokens that make other positions easier to predict, rather than prioritizing only easy tokens.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learned token-commitment schedules can reduce decoding rounds and enable faster parallel generation for mathematical reasoning and code tasks.
method: Construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal reduces uncertainty at other positions.
Distill these schedules into the model for faster parallel sampling.
Use KL-divergence regularization to help preserve generation quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations on math reasoning and code generation, with GSM8K speedups of 10.12× for LLaDA-8B-Instruct and 5.12× for Dream-7B-Instruct over baselines while maintaining superior task performance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify timing conditions or schedule-construction costs, so deployment speedups and training overhead require verification.
infographic.paper_title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models

title: Provably Efficient Q-learning for Robust Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Standard reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms based on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps. To address this issue, distributionally robust RL algorithms based on robust MDPs (RMDPs) have been proposed, for ensuring that agents can perform reliably to unpredictable conditions in real-world environments. Despite of the rich literature, \revision{an efficient model-free method is still lacking} for robust RL, particularly for Markovian data, which is more relevant in practical applications. In this work, we take a step towards settling this problem by proposing a sample efficient (asynchronous Q-learning) algorithm for robust RL. In particular, consider a $γ$-discounted infinite-horizon RMDP with state space $\mathcal{S}$ and action space $\mathcal{A}$, where the uncertainty set is specified by the total variation (TV) distance with uncertainty level $σ$. Assuming access to a single trajectory of Markovian samples induced by a behavior policy and the nominal transition kernel, the sample complexity of the proposed Q-learning algorithm --- to achieve an entrywise $\varepsilon$-approximation of the optimal Q-function --- is bounded by $$ \frac{1}{μ_{\mathsf{min}}\varepsilon^2(1-γ)^3\max\{1-γ,σ\}} + \frac{t_{\mathsf{mix}}}{μ_{\mathsf{min}}(1-γ)} $$ up to logarithmic factors. Here, $t_{\mathsf{mix}}$ and $μ_{\mathsf{min}}$ denote the mixing time and the minimum state-action occupancy probability of the sample trajectory, respectively. This result is nearly minimax optimal, with an additional factor of $\frac{1}{1-γ}$. Moreover, it achieves a significant improvement over existing bounds.

infographic.key_insight: A sample-efficient, model-free robust Q-learning algorithm learns from a single Markovian trajectory, with a theoretical guarantee within a factor of 1/(1−γ) of minimax optimality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets sim-to-real transition uncertainty, offering a route to policies that remain reliable when deployment dynamics differ from the nominal model.
method: Use asynchronous Q-learning in a discounted, infinite-horizon robust MDP.
Model transition uncertainty with total-variation neighborhoods of radius σ.
Learn from one trajectory generated by a behavior policy under nominal dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract gives a theoretical sample-complexity bound of Õ(1/[μ_min ε²(1−γ)³ max{1−γ,σ}] + t_mix/[μ_min(1−γ)]) for entrywise ε-accurate optimal Q-values; it reports no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The bound worsens with poor state-action coverage, slow trajectory mixing, and discount factors near one.
infographic.paper_title: Provably Efficient Q-learning for Robust Reinforcement Learning

title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models
authors: Yalu Ping, Chen Xuerong, Yu Dalei
abstract: Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.

infographic.key_insight: ReMAQ enables sequential model averaging for generalized linear models by using quadratic approximation to avoid revisiting the full historical dataset.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports computationally efficient prediction updates for high-volume streaming applications with multiple candidate models.
method: Approximate the GLM model-averaging objective with a quadratic formulation.
Update model-averaging weights through quadratic programming as each data batch arrives.
Establish asymptotic equivalence to full-data oracle weights and asymptotic optimality under regularity conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation studies and an Airline On-Time Performance Dataset application with favorable results, but provides no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical guarantees require regularity conditions; robustness to distribution shifts in real-world streams is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models

title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang
abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

infographic.key_insight: Accordion lets one mixture-of-experts language model serve five inference budgets by repeatedly executing fixed layer prefixes, improving performance as inference depth increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single shared-parameter model can offer multiple compute–quality settings, reducing the need to train and maintain separate models for different inference budgets.
method: Define five execution paths using fixed-prefix layer looping, with an unlooped minimum-budget path.
Jointly pretrain by sampling one budget per micro-batch and optimizing next-token prediction without cross-budget consistency losses.
Preserve all budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, integrating three domain experts via parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 3.6T pretraining tokens, increased depth improved the five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points; the middle budget captured 89% of that gain with half as many additional layer executions.
infographic.watch_item: Layer-execution counts are not direct latency measurements; deployment benefits require hardware-specific profiling of looping and mixture-of-experts routing.
infographic.paper_title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping

title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration
authors: Ruhao Liu, Qi Li, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang
abstract: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.

infographic.key_insight: DynaFlow learns to generate executable, task-specific multi-agent workflows rather than relying on predefined collaboration structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables adaptive orchestration of fixed sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification.
method: Let the main agent decide when to collaborate and synthesize executable workflows.
Use execution results and traces to guide subsequent reasoning and coordination.
Train only the main agent on distilled trajectories, then refine using examples filtered for premise, verification, and information-flow defects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six benchmarks covering math, scientific QA, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow reports 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, 10.90 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline using the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report orchestration latency or cost, leaving the deployment overhead of generated multi-agent workflows unclear.
infographic.paper_title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

title: On the Error Analysis of Triangular Transport Maps for Conditional Generation via MMD-based Objectives
authors: Michele Martino, Bamdad Hosseini, Amir Sagiv, Amirhossein Taghvaei
abstract: Conditional generative models parameterized by triangular transport maps are widely used for conditional sampling, yet theoretical guarantees on the quality of the conditional measures they produce remain scarce. We address this question for minimum divergence estimators of triangular maps. We use MMD-based objectives as a tractable setting in which the gap between joint and conditional errors can be analyzed precisely, and we measure performance through the average conditional estimation error, defined as the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the estimated and the true conditionals, averaged over the conditioning variable. We first show that the common practice of minimizing a joint MMD may fail to recover the conditionals: writing the joint and the conditional criteria as quadratic energies of the same conditional mean embedding residual, we prove that, for parametric classes, joint minimizers are generically inconsistent in the misspecified setting. We then analyze an estimator that directly minimizes the conditional criterion through a surrogate loss computable from joint target samples and reference samples. We prove a non-asymptotic error bound that decomposes the average conditional estimation error into approximation, estimation, and reference sampling errors, with fast rates independent of the ambient dimension in the parametric setting. Finally, for joint MMDs built from concentrating Gaussian kernels on the conditioning variable, we show that the joint criterion approximates a density-reweighted version of the conditional one, and we derive an error bound for the joint minimizer whose rate suffers from a curse of dimensionality in the conditioning variable. Our results suggest that training criteria for conditional generative models should target the conditional rather than the joint error, a principle that extends to other divergences and to dynamic transport.

infographic.key_insight: Minimizing joint MMD can fail to recover accurate conditional distributions, while directly targeting conditional MMD yields guarantees for triangular transport models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Conditional generators should use objectives aligned with conditional sampling accuracy rather than rely on joint distribution matching alone.
method: Express joint and conditional MMD criteria as quadratic energies of conditional mean embedding residuals.
Analyze a conditional-loss surrogate computable from joint target samples and reference samples.
Derive non-asymptotic error bounds and study joint MMD with concentrating Gaussian conditioning kernels.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical inconsistency results and error bounds separating approximation, estimation, and reference sampling errors, with dimension-independent fast rates in the parametric setting.
infographic.watch_item: Concentrating Gaussian kernels make joint MMD approximate a density-reweighted conditional criterion, but the resulting guarantee suffers from the conditioning dimension.
infographic.paper_title: On the Error Analysis of Triangular Transport Maps for Conditional Generation via MMD-based Objectives

title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
abstract: We consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, which incorporates a control potential into block updates while retaining the original objective, variables, and constraints. Under explicit control design conditions and the KL property, the control yields boundedness, finite length, whole-sequence convergence of the original variables, and convergence of objective values. At the limit, one limiting subgradient of the original objective vanishes on all effective comparison directions. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), CP decomposition, and independent-core matrix tri-factorization (NMTF) with $\ell_0$ norm sparsity constraints. We characterize their reconstruction-preserving scale degeneracies, proving that scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse and that full criticality forces such collapse. Explicit controls provide compact sublevel sets and a uniform positive lower bound on graph action, including with an independent Tucker core, while retaining genuine reconstruction-changing directions. Each block admits an explicit projection and a computable safe step parameter. For ordinary NMF and CP models, whole-sequence convergence to a full critical point follows. Experiments with direct safe updates demonstrate convergence, sustained graph action, and controlled factor and core scales.

infographic.key_insight: CBPL adds control to block updates to obtain bounded, convergent iterates under explicit design conditions and the KL property, without changing the original objective, variables, or constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method addresses scale degeneracy in graph-regularized sparse matrix and tensor factorizations while preserving meaningful reconstruction updates.
method: Incorporate a control potential into block proximal linearized updates.
Design controls for compact sublevel sets and uniformly positive graph action.
Use explicit block projections and computable safe step parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments showing convergence, sustained graph action, and controlled factor and core scales, but provides no quantitative results or dataset details.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence requires the stated control conditions and KL property; full critical-point convergence is established for ordinary NMF and CP, not claimed universally.
infographic.paper_title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
